newsitem.title: EGYPT: EU refuses to be mere paymaster in Mideast - Italy.
newsitem.headline: EU refuses to be mere paymaster in Mideast - Italy.

text.p: Italy said on Monday that Europe refused to be mere paymaster to the partners in Middle East peace talks and must eventually take on a political role to match its dominant economic presence.
But Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi told reporters in Cairo that Europe had no immediate ambitions to mediate directly between Israel and its Arab neighbours.

Israel rejected on Sunday a demand by French President Jacques Chirac that Europe act as joint sponsor of Middle East peace negotiations but said Europe still had an important role in supporting Middle East economies.
Prodi, speaking after talks with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, said it was unrealistic to try to separate political influence and economic contacts.

"Do you think that Europe will be forever the payer and that's all? Do you think this would be realistic -- that we shall go on paying for years and years and increasing our economic presence and just shut up?" he said.

"I know we can't pretend to be mediators in the process. But I doubt we would go on doing this job for an indefinite period. It's nice to have an uncle who pays for everything but this is only in tales, not in reality," he added.

The European Union is by far the largest single donor of aid to the Palestinian Authority, way ahead of the United States, and it is the biggest trading partner for most countries in the region, including Israel.
In the case of Egypt, Italy alone is the second largest importer of Egyptian goods and the biggest exporter to Egypt.
Prodi said the European Union's attempt to assert its presence in the Middle East was a long-term plan and it did not expect immediate results.
The European Union, at a meeting in Dublin last month, decided to appoint a special envoy to keep an eye on Middle East peace talks but it has not yet named the envoy.

"I never talked about mediation. Now it is a role of presence but it will increase in the future. When there is a presence of such a big entity as the European one the result sooner or later will come. We are not pushing for immediate results," he said.
"There is already a strong presence of Europe here. We must translate into action what already exists," he added.
He said that President Mubarak was enouraging Europe but was also pessimistic that it could achieve quick results.
Mubarak tried to persuade Prodi that Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi had changed his attitude to the West and was now trying to be cooperative, Prodi added.

Libya, also an important trading partner for Italy, was been under limited U.N. sanctions since 1992 because it refuses to let Britain or the United States try two Libyan men accused of blowing up a Pan Am plane over Scotland in 1988.
"President Mubarak insisted on the limits of the politics of embargo, especially with Libya," Prodi said.

"He presented his opinion that now Gaddafi is changing his politics and trying to have a much more cooperative policy with the Western world, with Europe, and has done positive and concrete steps in this direction," he added.
The prime minister did not give his own opinion on whether Gaddafi had changed and deserved to have the sanctions lifted.
He said Italy hoped to become the biggest market for Egyptian exports and would take an active part in next month's Middle east and North Africa economic conference in Cairo.
Prodi arrived in Italy on Sunday afternoon and left for Rome shortly after his news conference.
